theme: Crossing the Jordan; circumcision renewed; the Passover kept
readingInstruction: Read Joshua 3:1-5:15. It is a long reading, but the three chapters tell one story: the nation crosses the Jordan, builds a memorial, is renewed in covenant signs, and meets the commander of the LORD’s army. Notice how often the ark, the stones, and the Passover remind Israel what God has done.
settingTheScene: The spies have returned from Jericho with good news: the inhabitants are melting in fear. But there is still a river between Israel and the land, and in the spring it is at flood stage. Forty years earlier, God parted the Red Sea for their parents. Now he will do something similar for the children, but it will happen in a different way. The priests carrying the ark will step into the water first. Once across, Israel will pause at Gilgal for three acts that prepare them for the conquest: they will set up a memorial, renew circumcision, and keep the Passover. Only then will the commander of the LORD’s army appear. The order matters. Israel is not ready to fight until they are ready to worship.
observation: The people are told to follow the ark at a distance of about two thousand cubits, so everyone can see where it goes (3:3-4).
Joshua tells them, “Consecrate yourselves, for tomorrow the LORD will do wonders among you” (3:5).
The waters stop only when the priests’ feet touch the edge of the Jordan, even though it is overflowing its banks (3:13-15).
The priests stand firm in the middle of the dry riverbed until all Israel has crossed (3:17).
Twelve stones are taken from the Jordan to Gilgal, as a memorial “so that all the peoples of the earth may know that the hand of the LORD is mighty” (4:20-24).
The generation born in the wilderness had not been circumcised, so Joshua circumcises them at Gilgal (5:2-7).
The manna ceases the day after they eat the produce of the land (5:12).
Joshua meets a man with a drawn sword who says he is “commander of the army of the LORD” and tells Joshua to remove his sandals, because the place is holy (5:13-15).
interpretation:
The crossing of the Jordan deliberately echoes the crossing of the Red Sea. The author wants us to see that the God who brought Israel out of Egypt is the same God who now brings them in. But there are differences. At the Red Sea, Moses stretched out a staff and the waters parted, and Israel crossed while the enemy chased them. At the Jordan, no enemy pursues. The challenge is not escape but entry. And the miracle begins only when the priests step in. They have to walk into a flooded river before the water stops. Faith precedes sight. God does not part the waters in advance. He asks his people to take a step of trust, and then he acts.

The ark is the center of the story. It is the symbol of God’s throne and presence, and it goes first. The people follow at a distance, which keeps the focus on the ark and not on the carriers. This is the pattern of the whole conquest: Israel does not win because of its army but because God goes before them. The lesson for every believer is simple. We do not go anywhere that God has not first gone.

Then the people build a memorial. Twelve stones, one for each tribe, are taken from the middle of the Jordan and piled up at Gilgal. The purpose is explained twice: so that future children will ask, “What do these stones mean?” and the parents will tell them the story. God’s people are a remembering people. Spiritual memory does not happen automatically. It needs signs, stories, and rituals that pass faith from one generation to the next. This is the logic of baptism and the Lord’s Supper, and it is the reason your own daily reading matters.

Chapter 5 is surprising. Israel has crossed the river, and the Canaanite kings are afraid, yet Joshua stops to circumcise every man. It seems like a terrible time to put the army out of action. But God is teaching a priority. The sign of the Abrahamic covenant had been neglected in the wilderness. Before the people take the land, they must renew the mark that says they belong to God. Then they celebrate Passover and eat the produce of the land. The manna stops. God has provided what they need in the wilderness, and now he provides from the inheritance he promised.

Finally, a mysterious figure appears. Joshua, a warrior, asks whether he is for Israel or for their enemies. The answer is “No.” The commander of the LORD’s army has not come to take sides. He has come to take command. Joshua falls on his face and removes his sandals, just as Moses did at the burning bush. The figure is likely a pre-incarnate appearance of the Son, the one who leads God’s armies. Joshua is not the real captain of the host. The real captain has arrived.
connection: The crossing of the Jordan echoes the crossing of the Red Sea (Exodus 14) and anticipates Elijah and Elisha crossing the same river (2 Kings 2) and the baptism of Jesus there (Matthew 3). The memorial stones recall Deuteronomy 6:20-25. Circumcision renews the sign of Genesis 17. The manna’s end ties to Exodus 16. The commander’s command to remove sandals repeats Exodus 3:5, and the same figure appears as the “angel of the LORD” throughout the Old Testament.
application:
First, think about what step of faith God may be asking you to take before he shows you the outcome. The priests had to get their feet wet. Ask the Lord for the courage to take one step this week.

Second, build your own memorial. Write down three things God has done for you in the last year, and put the list somewhere you will see it. Tell someone younger in the faith about one of them.

Third, ask yourself what must be set right before you can move forward. Israel could not conquer until the covenant sign was renewed. Is there something in your relationship with God that has been neglected?

Fourth, notice that the commander is not on your side. He is in charge. Bow to him in prayer this week and ask him what he wants, rather than asking him to bless your plans.
prayerPrompts: Ask God to teach you to follow where he leads.
Thank him for what he has done, and ask him to help you tell the story to someone else.
Tell him about a “Jordan” you are facing.
